items.author: Cointelegraph
items.context: @Cointelegraph (2.925.584 seguidores), en inglés, con imagen: «JUST IN: US DOJ files to recover over $1.1 billion in USDC stolen by North Korean hackers in the $6 billion Binance hack, with nearly $3 billion in crypto already frozen, seized or returned.» Post de ~55 min con 75 likes, 15 reposts, 32 respuestas y 23.334 vistas. Ángulo: lo que se recupera tras un hackeo depende de emisores que pueden congelar (USDC) y de exchanges; custodia propia = nadie congela, nadie recupera.
items.suggested_text:
Notice where the recovery actually comes from. Most of what gets "frozen, seized or returned" after a hack is stablecoins with an issuer that can blacklist addresses, plus exchanges that cooperate. USDC can be frozen because Circle controls the contract: the same switch that helps victims here can lock anyone else out tomorrow.

Coins sitting on an exchange are a claim on that exchange, and the wallets pooling everyone's funds are exactly what state-backed groups like North Korea's go after. Bitcoin in keys you control works the other way: nobody can freeze it on you, and nobody can claw it back for you either.

That trade-off is the whole custody question, and most people only think it through after a headline like this one.
